projects.title: Predictive Text Engine
projects.oneLiner: A text prediction system exploring algorithms, language patterns, and efficient suggestions.
projects.summary: A problem-solving project focused on turning data structures and prediction logic into a practical interaction.
projects.problem: The goal was to predict likely next words and provide autocomplete while handling different n-gram approaches and text filtering.
projects.whatIBuilt: Worked with bigram and trigram models, the Brown corpus, profanity filtering, and Trie-based autocomplete. The project evolved from a Java/JavaFX version into a Python/Tkinter implementation.
projects.learned: How language can be represented computationally, how different n-gram approaches behave, and how data structures such as Tries can support fast autocomplete.
projects.overview: A predictive text engine built on Markov chains. It is trained with bigrams and trigrams, adds prefix-based autocomplete, and shows live next-word suggestions in a Tkinter desktop app.
features: Text cleaning pipeline: punctuation removal, lowercasing and tokenization
Bigram and trigram models with normalized transition probabilities
Top 3–5 next-word suggestions in real time
Prefix-based autocomplete while typing
Model selector: Bigram, Trigram or Both
Training on the NLTK Brown corpus plus a custom corpus file
Unit tests with pytest
howItWorks: The Brown corpus and corpus/corpus.txt are cleaned and merged into one training set.
Bigram and trigram frequency tables are built and turned into probability distributions.
For a prediction the engine checks the trigram context first, falls back to the bigram, then to prefix autocomplete, and ranks results by probability.
In the Tkinter GUI, every key press triggers the engine and suggestions appear under the input field.

screenshots.alt: Predictive Text Engine main window with input box, live predictions and model selector

projects.title: Contract and Payroll Management System
projects.oneLiner: A JavaFX desktop application for managing employee contracts, payroll, requests, documents, attendance, shifts, leave and training in a company.
projects.overview: An interactive system for managing staff contracts and salaries in a company, built by a team of six for the Human-Computer Interaction (Komunikimi Njeri-Kompjuter) course at FIEK, University of Prishtina. Administrators manage the organisation’s HR and payroll records, while employees see their own contracts, salaries, documents, requests and shifts. The interface is available in Albanian and English.
features: Login and registration with SHA-256 password hashing and role-based dashboards for admins and employees
Albanian and English interface, switchable from the login screen
Admin dashboard with active workers, pending requests, this month’s salaries, ongoing trainings and a salary trend chart
Management of workers, users, departments, positions, contracts, salaries, bonuses and deductions
Contract search, expiry view, contract statistics chart and export of contract details to PDF
Requests with approval or rejection, leave, overtime, attendance, shifts, trainings and employee evaluations
Employee area: profile summary, own contracts and salaries, requests, shifts and requests for contract changes
Uploading, storing and opening personal documents (PDF) from inside the app
howItWorks: It is a desktop application, not a web app: FXML views are handled by JavaFX controllers, which call service classes for validation and business logic.
Services call repository classes that run SQL against PostgreSQL through JDBC with prepared statements and map results into model classes; create and update operations use DTO classes.

The normalized PostgreSQL schema has 18 tables, among them departments, positions, users, workers, contracts, salaries, bonuses, deductions, leave, overtime, documents, attendance, shifts, evaluations, trainings and requests.

After login the user is kept in a SessionManager and sent to the admin or employee dashboard by role; texts come from Java ResourceBundle files for Albanian and English, and contract PDFs are produced with iText.

teamInfo.note: Team project for the Human-Computer Interaction (Komunikimi Njeri-Kompjuter) course at FIEK, University of Prishtina. The repository is owned by Engji Osmani; Erza is one of six contributors and set up the initial project, the PostgreSQL connection and the SQL schema, and worked mostly on contracts, documents, shifts and the dashboards.

projects.title: CollabAI
projects.oneLiner: A full-stack, AI-powered project management platform for organizing teams, projects and tasks, with a built-in AI assistant that uses RAG and semantic search over the organization’s data.
projects.overview: CollabAI is a full-stack project management platform for organizing teams, projects, tasks and collaboration, with a built-in AI assistant powered by retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and semantic search. It is built for multi-tenant use: one platform can serve several organizations while keeping each organization’s data isolated.
features: JWT authentication with registration, token refresh and blacklisting, and password reset by email
Organizations, workspaces and email invitations with scoped roles (Org Admin, Workspace Admin, Manager, Member)
Projects and tasks with status, priority, labels, assignee, due date and file attachments
Task comments with an activity log, in-app notifications and an admin audit trail
Dashboard with a summary of tasks, projects and team activity
AI chatbot, text analysis (summary, action items, sentiment), semantic search across tasks and comments, and RAG question answering over the organization’s own project data
howItWorks: A React single-page app talks to a Django REST Framework API under /api/v1/, sending a JWT and an organization ID with every request.
Middleware validates the token and resolves the tenant; the backend re-checks tenant scope and role-based access before every response.
Views and serializers hand work to service classes; data lives in PostgreSQL, with Redis for caching and Celery for background jobs.

For AI answers, organization data is embedded with sentence-transformers and stored in a Redis vector store; relevant items are retrieved and sent as context to a LLaMA 3.1 model through the Groq API.

items: GitHub Actions (tests, lint, Cypress E2E, Docker build)

projects.title: ParkEasy
projects.oneLiner: A cross-platform mobile app for finding, reserving and managing parking in Kosovo, with separate experiences for drivers, parking owners and admins.
projects.overview: ParkEasy is a mobile parking management app built with React Native, Expo and Firebase for the Mobile Application Programming course at FIEK. Drivers can discover parking nearby on a map, search, reserve and manage bookings; parking owners manage their spaces and reservations; administrators review parking requests and manage users.
features: Login and registration with role-based access for Users, Owners and Admins, plus Google sign-in
Nearby view: real-time map of parking spots with reservation from the map
Location-based search for parking spaces
Reserve, edit and cancel bookings, with booking history
Favorites for saving preferred parking locations
Profile with photo upload and notification settings, and in-app notifications for bookings
Owner dashboard for parking spaces, earnings and reservations
Admin panel for parking requests, parking lists, reservations and user management
howItWorks: The app uses Expo Router with separate route groups for authentication, the user tabs (Nearby, Search, Bookings, Favorites, Profile), the owner area and the admin area.
Firebase Authentication handles sign-in, and Firestore and Storage hold parkings, bookings, users and photos with real-time updates.
Maps are built with react-native-maps and Leaflet; distances to parkings are calculated with haversine-distance and the device location from expo-location.
Booking confirmations and updates are delivered with expo-notifications; behaviour is covered by Jest tests with React Native Testing Library.

teamInfo.note: Team project for the Mobile Application Programming course at FIEK. The repository is owned by Edonita Gashi; Erza is one of six developers.

projects.title: DCADD Master Project
projects.oneLiner: Terraform infrastructure on AWS for a highly available web application: a multi-AZ VPC, private EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling Group behind an Application Load Balancer, deployed with GitHub Actions.
projects.overview: Terraform code that provisions AWS infrastructure for a highly available web application, built for the DCADD Master Project course. It creates a multi-AZ network, runs the app on private EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer, and deploys changes automatically with GitHub Actions.
features: VPC (10.0.0.0/16) with three public and three private subnets across eu-central-1a, 1b and 1c
Internet-facing Application Load Balancer on HTTP port 80
Auto Scaling Group of t3.micro instances (min 2, desired 3, max 6) in private subnets with no public IPs
NAT Gateway for outbound internet from the private subnets
Security groups that allow HTTP to the instances only from the load balancer
Remote Terraform state in S3; configuration through variables with sensible defaults
howItWorks: Terraform files are split by concern: networking, security, compute, load balancing, data (Amazon Linux 2023 AMI lookup) and outputs.
Each EC2 instance boots with a user-data script that deploys the course’s group web application.
On a pull request, GitHub Actions runs terraform fmt, init, validate and plan; on merge to main it runs terraform apply.
After apply, the load balancer’s DNS name is output as the public URL of the app.

teamInfo.note: Individual project by Erza for the DCADD Master Project course.

projects.title: Text Rule Processor
projects.oneLiner: A rule-based content filter web app: users define rules that detect patterns in text and mark them with highlights or tooltips, with a history of processed text.
projects.overview: A rule-based content filter web app. Users define rules that detect patterns in text and mark every match with a coloured highlight or a tooltip label. It was created as an internship assignment to demonstrate full-stack development.
features: Create, edit, delete, enable and disable rules
Match types: contains, starts with and exact match
Actions: highlight with a custom colour, or tooltip with a label
Process typed text or an uploaded .txt file against all enabled rules, with match statistics
History of processed text that can be viewed and deleted
Rule priority, search and filter, preview before saving, and toast notifications
howItWorks: The React frontend calls a Node.js and Express API.
The API stores rules and history in PostgreSQL (Neon or local) through node-postgres; tables are created automatically on startup.
POST /process runs the text against all enabled rules and returns the matches, which the frontend renders as highlights and tooltips.

teamInfo.note: Individual project by Erza, built as an internship assignment.

projects.title: Maze Solver Visualizer
projects.oneLiner: An interactive maze editor and pathfinding visualizer that uses A* search with a Manhattan-distance heuristic to find the shortest path.
projects.overview: An interactive maze editor and pathfinding visualizer. You draw a grid maze, place a start and a goal, and the A* algorithm finds and draws the shortest path. It demonstrates heuristic search, cost functions and path reconstruction visually.
features: Grid maze editor: left click toggles walls, Shift + left click sets the start, right click sets the goal
A* search with a Manhattan-distance heuristic and 4-directional movement
Shortest path highlighted, with its length shown in the status bar
Status messages for invalid setups (start or goal on a wall, no path found)
Dark-themed Tkinter interface, plus a console version
howItWorks: Each cell is scored with f(n) = g(n) + h(n): the cost so far plus the Manhattan distance to the goal.
A min-heap priority queue (heapq) always expands the most promising cell next.
Because the heuristic is admissible, A* returns an optimal shortest path when one exists; the path is then reconstructed and drawn on the grid.

about.heading: Somewhere between two worlds, I found software engineering.
about.lead: I am, in many ways, a product of two very different kinds of work.
paragraphs: My father is a mechanic; my mother is a tailor. One world of engines and tools, the other of fabrics and patterns. From my father I learned the value of showing up, being patient, and finishing what you start—the kind of work ethic that comes from fixing things carefully, not rushing past the hard parts.

From my mother I inherited a different kind of attention: creativity, and the habit of noticing small details. Growing up around sewing, patterns, measurements, and handmade work taught me that creating something takes both an idea and the patience to turn that idea into something real.

Somewhere between those two sides, I found software. I enjoy understanding how things work, breaking complex problems into smaller pieces, and building solutions that make sense. I care about how something works, but also how it feels, looks, and comes together as a whole—because building well, for me, has always meant both logic and care.
about.quote: "I don't know yet" is not a weakness. It is the beginning of figuring it out.
about.beyondLead: These interests may seem unrelated to software, but they all share something: patience, curiosity, and the satisfaction of creating or understanding something.
about.motto: Good enough is not good enough.
about.mottoWhy: It is not only about finishing the job. It means always trying to improve, in work and in life, and never stopping just because something looks good enough.
about.funFact: I still mix up left and right. As a kid I came up with my own little conspiracy theory about it, and even though I know it makes no sense, I’ve never quite managed to shake it.

purpose.label: Where I want to go
purpose.heading: Something I care about beyond code.
paragraphs: I grew up close to a child with Down syndrome, and I saw what daily life can look like for a family like theirs. In Kosovo, the right support is hard to find, and many families are left to figure it out alone.

I study software engineering, and I love it. Someday I want to work with organizations that support children with autism, Down syndrome, and other special needs, building tools that save teachers time, apps families can actually use, and interfaces that feel calm. I am still at the beginning.
I want to build things well, for people who are too often forgotten.
